opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the motivation behind COLM was really that language modeling has become this enormous area, and yet there wasn't a single venue that felt like home for people working on it directly. If you look at where these papers were landing, they were scattered. Some went to NeurIPS or ICML, which are huge general machine learning conferences, and some went to ACL or EMNLP, which come out of a computational linguistics tradition. Both of those communities are wonderful, but neither was quite designed around the questions people are asking now about language models themselves.

So what we wanted was a place where the core object of study is the language model. That covers a really broad range of work: pretraining and data, alignment, evaluation, interpretability, efficiency, safety, societal impact, applications. The idea is that someone thinking about scaling laws and someone thinking about how these models get used in education or law should be in the same room and talking to each other, because those questions really are connected now.

We also wanted it to be smaller and more focused than the mega-conferences, so you can actually find the people you want to talk to and have real conversations rather than wandering a convention center with fifteen thousand people. And we care a lot about it being interdisciplinary. We want linguists, cognitive scientists, social scientists, and people in the humanities to feel welcome, not just ML engineers.

The last piece is openness. A lot of the most important work in this area right now happens inside a handful of companies, and much of it isn't published. Part of the goal is to build a strong academic and open-science community around language modeling, where people share findings, release artifacts, and hold the work to rigorous scientific standards. We want it to be a place where careful, reproducible science about these systems gets rewarded.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the honest origin story is a little mundane. A bunch of us were sitting around, and this was in the period right after ChatGPT, and we were noticing that the work we cared about didn't really have a home. If you were doing language modeling research, you could go to ACL or EMNLP, which are NLP conferences, or you could go to NeurIPS or ICML, which are machine learning conferences. And both of those are great venues, but language modeling had become this thing that cut across all of them and also didn't fit neatly in any of them. The NLP community was, I think, a little bit in shock about what had happened, and the ML community treated language models as one application among many. So a paper on, say, how data mixtures affect pretraining, or how to evaluate a chat model, or the societal implications of deploying these systems at scale, would get reviewed by people who weren't really thinking about those questions day to day.

So the community we wanted was one where the object of study is the language model itself. Not NLP broadly, not ML broadly, but this specific artifact that has turned out to be enormously important and that we honestly don't understand very well. And I mean that in a wide sense. We wanted people who do scaling and systems work talking to people who do alignment, talking to people who study these models from a linguistics or cognitive science perspective, talking to people thinking about policy and misuse. Those groups mostly don't go to the same conferences right now, and I think that's bad for the field.

The other thing we were pretty deliberate about is that we wanted it to be a place where academics and smaller labs could still participate meaningfully. There was a real worry, and there still is, that language modeling becomes a field where the interesting work only happens inside a handful of companies, and the rest of us just write papers about their APIs. I don't think that's inevitable. There's a huge amount of important science to do that doesn't require a thousand GPUs, on evaluation, on interpretability, on data, on smaller open models. And a conference can shape what counts as a contribution. If reviewers value careful, reproducible, open work, people will do more of it.

And then there was a kind of cultural thing too. The big conferences had gotten so large that they'd lost a bit of the feeling of being a community, where you actually know the people in the room and the conversations in the hallway are as valuable as the talks. We wanted something that felt more like a field getting together than a trade show. Whether we've pulled that off, I think you'd have to ask the attendees, but that was the intent. Small enough to be a community, broad enough to include everybody who is actually serious about understanding these models.

r001.rationale: It describes a community giving work researchers care about a home and welcoming a broad range of research on language models, including work that does not require large resources.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes the intended focus on language models themselves from NLP broadly and says language modeling does not fit neatly within traditional NLP venues.

r003.rationale: It does not mention ICLR or characterize the topics studied there.

r004.rationale: It discusses academics and smaller labs, but does not say COLM’s program chairs bring academics and industry researchers together.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re trying to create a community where language modeling is the shared interest, but people can come at it from very different directions. There are people thinking about the science of these models, people building systems, and people asking what they’re useful for and where they fail. I’d like those people to be in conversation with each other.

And I want it to be a place where you can contribute without having the resources to train the biggest model. A careful experiment, an interesting question, or a result that challenges something we all assume should have a place. To me, the opportunity is to build a conference that’s rigorous but also welcoming, where people can talk openly about what they’re learning and what they still don’t understand.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the goal is to create a community where language modeling is treated as a broad research area, and where people working on different parts of it can really talk to each other. There are people interested in the science of these models, people building systems, people studying data, and people thinking about how we evaluate and use them. We want those groups in the same room.

And I’d like it to be a place where you can contribute a good idea without having the resources to train the biggest model. A careful experiment, an interesting theoretical result, or a finding that challenges what everybody assumes should all have a place. The hope is to build a conference that’s rigorous, but also welcoming—especially for students—and focused on exchanging ideas.
